April 26

Edwards out weeks as injuries mount for Wolves

The Minnesota Timberwolves won the battle on Saturday night, with a stirring Game 4 victory over Denver that brought the team within a win of the second round.

But they might have lost the war.

On Saturday night, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Donte DiVincenzo had torn his right Achilles and would miss the rest of the postseason. And on Sunday morning, he reported that four-time All-Star Anthony Edwards would miss multiple weeks after hyperextending his left knee.

Losing a starting backcourt in one fell swoop would hurt any team in the playoffs, but it should be especially tough on Minnesota. The Timberwolves rely on a strong core, with little depth behind it; entering Saturday's games, only seven Wolves had averaged more than 10 minutes per game in the playoffs. By comparison, 10 members for both the Oklahoma City Thunder and San Antonio Spurs played more than that, and even the injury-riddled Lakers had eight.

With Edwards and DiVincenzo out, Minnesota's entire rotation and offensive gameplan will shift. Ayo Dosunmu -- fresh off a 43-point outburst -- and Bones Hyland are the likely replacement starters, with some combination of Mike Conley, Terrence Shannon Jr. (who received his first playoff minutes in Game 4) and Kyle Anderson receiving more minutes off the bench.

That might not be a tenable arrangement on offense, unless Dosunmu can continue posting career highs in points going forward. There's very little shooting and playmaking talent left in Minnesota's lineup, and Julius Randle -- who has been only OK against Denver, averaging 17.5 points and 3.5 assists per game on subpar efficiency -- will need to step up in Edwards' stead.

But all isn't lost for the Timberwolves, at least against the Nuggets. Surprisingly, lineups without DiVincenzo and Edwards held their own in the regular season, with a plus-3.0 net rating, per Cleaning the Glass (which removes garbage time). Those groups excelled on defense. And as long as Rudy Gobert and Jaden McDaniels remain on the floor, Minnesota will retain its top two options to guard Nikola Jokic and Jamal Murray, respectively.

Minnesota is already winning because of its defense. The Timberwolves have a 112.3 offensive rating in the playoffs, which is worse than their regular-season mark (115.6). But they've held the Nuggets, who led the league with a 121.1 offensive rating in the regular season, to just 105.2 points per 100 possessions in the playoffs.

It might not be the most probable outcome, but they have a real chance to keep Denver's offense sufficiently in check to sneak out one more win in three tries.

Beyond that, Minnesota is likely in trouble. Without Edwards for multiple weeks, the Timberwolves might need to hope that the Portland Trail Blazers upset San Antonio to have a chance to reach the conference finals for the third consecutive season. -- Zach Kram

April 25

Wolves' DiVincenzo tears Achilles in Game 4

Minnesota Timberwolves guard Donte DiVincenzo will miss the rest of this postseason and at least a large chunk of next season after tearing his right Achilles just over a minute into Game 4 against the Denver Nuggets. The injury was first reported by ESPN's Shams Charania.

It's difficult to say whether that injury is a bigger blow to the Timberwolves or to DiVincenzo's own career path.

Due to his availability and shooting skill, DiVincenzo was a crucial contributor for Minnesota this season. He was one of just four players in the NBA to start all 82 games, and he offered a skill set otherwise missing from the players who surround Anthony Edwards in Minnesota's starting lineup. DiVincenzo shot 38% on 3-pointers this season and made 3.0 per game, which is more than Julius Randle, Jaden McDaniels and Rudy Gobert combined.

The Timberwolves had a plus-6.0 net rating with DiVincenzo on the court in the regular season, versus a minus-2.0 mark without him. That was the largest differential on the team. And in a very small sample of three playoff games, that gap widened: Minnesota was plus-20.7 with DiVincenzo and minus-26.3 without him.

Ayo Dosunmu fit in well in Minnesota after arriving via midseason trade, and he will presumably replace DiVincenzo in the starting lineup for the remainder of Minnesota's playoff run. Dosunmu is an accurate shooter (44% on 3s this season) but on much lower volume, and defenses are less likely to worry about him on the perimeter. According to the new "average gravity" statistic at NBA.com, DiVincenzo ranked in the 77th percentile among qualified players this season, while Dosunmu was in the 56th percentile.

And although the Timberwolves' starting unit might not be compromised too severely with Dosunmu in DiVincenzo's place -- if Edwards, who also left Saturday's Game 4 early, is also out for an extended period, then the Timberwolves will be severely compromised regardless -- the ripple effects could be catastrophic for Minnesota's bench. In the first three games against the Nuggets, only seven Timberwolves averaged more than 10 minutes per game: the five starters, Dosunmu and former Sixth Man award winner Naz Reid.

Beyond that core, the Timberwolves will have to rely on the unpredictable Bones Hyland and veterans Mike Conley and Kyle Anderson to absorb playing time. They might not have the depth to withstand the loss of any member of their main group.

And for the 29-year-old DiVincenzo individually, the injury doesn't just bring his 2025-26 season to an abrupt end, but it also potentially cuts short his prime.

Several years ago, DiVincenzo missed half of the 2021-22 season due to injury, which hurt his free agency case the following summer. And now he'll miss the rest of this season and most or all of the 2026-27 campaign, when he'll make $12.5 million in the final season of his current deal. -- Zach Kram

Could Dame return this postseason?

The plan has always been for Portland Trail Blazers guard Damian Lillard to rehabilitate his ruptured Achilles tendon and return next season.

That's still the plan. But this week, when Blazers head coach Tiago Splitter was asked if there's a possibility for Lillard to return during these playoffs, he didn't completely rule it out.

"Probably not," Splitter told reporters in Portland on Thursday.

Lillard has been seen publicly working out during practices and before games, in addition to extensive training on his own.

A source close to Lillard reiterated to ESPN that the plan is still for Lillard to continue his rehabilitation and return next season, but acknowledged that could be reconsidered if the Trail Blazers advance further in the playoffs.

Lillard has been out since rupturing his Achilles tendon during the first round of the playoffs last season when he was a member of the Milwaukee Bucks. He won the NBA's 3-point contest at the All-Star Game in February. -- Ramona Shelburne

April 23

Austin Reaves upgraded to questionable for Game 3
Lakers guard Austin Reaves has not played since he suffered Grade 2 left oblique muscle injury on April 2. The team announced on April 4 that he would miss at least the rest of the regular season. He was upgraded to probable on Thursday as the series shifts to Houston for Friday's Game 3 with the Lakers looking to take a 3-0 lead.

Durant questionable for Game 3
Kevin Durant, who made his Houston Rockets playoff debut in Game 2 after missing Game 1 with a right knee contusion, is now listed as questionable heading into Friday's Game 3 with a left ankle sprain. Embiid upgraded to doubtful for Game 3
The Philadelphia 76ers upgraded star center Joel Embiid to doubtful Thursday evening ahead of Friday's Game 3 at home against the Boston Celtics.

Embiid had an emergency appendectomy two weeks ago in Houston, and has been out since, although he appeared on the bench for last week's play-in victory at home against the Orlando Magic.

Warriors not rushing Kerr on decision
Steve Kerr has made no decision yet in regard to his future coaching the Golden State Warriors, and the two sides don't expect to come to any firm determination until next week at the earliest, team sources told ESPN.

Kerr said he needed a week or two for the necessary space, contemplation and bigger picture conversations before deciding whether to seek another contract with the Warriors or walk away from coaching entirely, perhaps into the media space.

The Warriors were eliminated on Friday in a play-in loss to the Phoenix Suns. They've spent this past week conducting exit interviews with players and staffers, and are gearing up for the offseason. Kerr's future is the first domino, but management doesn't plan to rush Kerr, who just finished his 12th season as head coach.

Kerr's contemplation will continue through the weekend.

"It's April," one team source said. "We don't need to rush." -- Anthony Slater

Bucks to hire Taylor Jenkins as next coach
The Milwaukee Bucks are hiring former Memphis Grizzlies coach Taylor Jenkins, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania and Ramona Shelburne. Jenkins, who will replace Doc Rivers, coached the Grizzlies for six seasons and led them to three playoff appearances.

Bucks management met with Jenkins last week in Memphis and this week in Milwaukee, sources said, to secure his commitment.

OKC's Williams sustained Grade 1 sprain

Thunder guard Jalen Williams has suffered a Grade 1 sprain to his left hamstring and will be reevaluated on a weekly basis. Williams, who was limited to 33 games in an injury-riddled regular season, had 22 points, seven rebounds and six assists in the Thunder's Game 1 blowout win and then 19 points on 7-of-11 shooting and four assists in 23 minutes in Game 2 before leaving with the injury in the third quarter.

Game 3 is Saturday in Phoenix at 3:30 p.m. ET on NBC.

San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama, in concussion protocol since a fall in the first half of Game 2, will travel with the team to Portland for Games 3-4, sources told ESPN's Shams Charania. The Spurs blew a 14-point lead in the Game 2 loss. The series is tied 1-1.

Inside the highlight reel that saved the Magic's season
How did the Orlando Magic turn things around -- and stun the Detroit Pistons in Game 1? It started with a three-minute video a week ago, according to a story published Wednesday from ESPN's Ohm Youngmisuk:

Last Friday morning, before the Magic's biggest shootaround of the season at their team facility, coach Jamahl Mosley showed his players a video, but not the usual film breakdown of the opponent. Instead, he played a three-minute highlight reel of some of his players' own NCAA tournament magic from back in the day.

Each player who had been in the tournament had two clips each in the video made by the team's video coordinator: Jonathan Isaac throwing down a dunk while at Florida State, Moritz Wagner hitting a 3 while being fouled for Michigan and Desmond Bane drilling a deep 3 for TCU. The highlight reel continued with Tristan da Silva at Colorado, Franz Wagner at Michigan, Wendell Carter Jr. at Duke and others.

The Warriors' summer of uncertainty starts with Steve Kerr
ESPN's Ramona Shelburne and Anthony Slater detailed the upcoming summer for the Golden State Warriors, an offseason that could lead to immense change for a franchise that has won four NBA titles in the past 11 seasons. What could be next for Stephen Curry, Draymond Green and coach Steve Kerr? An excerpt on the end of the Warriors' season:

Two nights later, their season ended at the hands of an upstart, younger Phoenix Suns team. The Warriors lost 111-96. It wasn't competitive. Curry scored just 17 points, on 25% shooting.
It was the Warriors' third consecutive appearance in the play-in tournament, and their second time in three years missing the playoffs entirely. Inside the organization, they've long known that, despite stretches of play that remind everyone of their game-changing past, like that fourth quarter against the Clippers, this team, with two aging icons on the wrong side of the actuarial table, is nowhere near good enough to win a title.

As their season came to a close, the trio of elder statesmen still fighting for it gathered on the sideline, perhaps for the final time.

"I don't know what's going to happen next," Kerr said Friday night. His right arm was on Green's shoulder, his left on Curry's. "But I love you guys to death."

Not just the Bam Adebayo game two years ago where he thought he got fouled and tripped Bam. But in February, he did this to Jabari Smith Jr. against the Rockets. Almost the same type of play. Why LaMelo's flagrant 2 falls into a gray area
The NBA retroactively assessed Charlotte Hornets guard LaMelo Ball with a flagrant foul 2 for tripping Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo in Tuesday's Eastern Conference play-in game, which Charlotte won in overtime thanks to Ball's last-second layup.

But for the Heat and their fans, it doesn't erase Adebayo's injury, it doesn't remove Ball from Friday's 8-9 game against the Orlando Magic and it all but certainly won't impact the Hornets should they reach the first round.

That's because one quirk of the tournament's addition is that, not unlike the NBA Cup title game, the play-in tournament lives as its own statistical entity. They are neither playoff nor regular-season games, with no bearing on postseason and regular-season stats or awards.

That's also the case with flagrant foul points, which can have a massive impact when they start to add up. In 2016, Draymond Green was suspended for Game 5 of the NBA Finals for accumulating four flagrant points over the course of the postseason, something that helped Cleveland pull off its stunning 3-1 comeback.

While the Hornets' playoff stay isn't likely to last as long -- Charlotte needs to win Friday just to set up a first-round meeting with the top-seeded Detroit Pistons -- Ball entering the playoffs with two flagrant points would have at least given heft to the belated punishment.

Instead, the decision felt fairly hollow. And in asking sources around the league Wednesday ahead of the NBA's announcement that Ball wouldn't be suspended, opinions were mixed. Some argued that a hefty fine would suffice, because you shouldn't retroactively remove him from the next game because of Adebayo's unfortunate injury. Others argued the opposite, saying he should have to sit out Friday's win-and-in showdown.

None of it, however, will reverse the agonizing end to Miami's season.

"I'm not really thinking about that anymore," Heat coach Erik Spoelstra told reporters Thursday during the team's exit interviews. "I don't think [Ball] is a dirty player. It should have been caught in the moment, and it wasn't. And you move on." -- Tim Bontemps

April 8

The NBA's take on tanking

ESPN's Anthony Slater talked to players, coaches and executives about how they feel about tanking in the NBA and the future it has in the league.

In ESPN's conversations with dozens of players, coaches and front office executives, a consistent theme emerged: Nobody likes it -- "I hate it," Golden State Warriors coach Steve Kerr said -- but not many deny it is often the most prudent team-building path when stuck near the bottom. Different seasons and different drafts will generate different forms, but everyone agrees it'll continue until the NBA figures out either the proper rules or punishments to curb it.

"These teams are doing the whole gamut: sitting guys in the fourth, playing analytically bad lineups, drawing up plays for bad shots," one Western Conference general manager said. "The creativity is impressive and I don't blame them. It's the best strategy to get better. Look at all the most promising teams in the league: Thunder, Spurs, Pistons, Rockets, Hornets. Years of being bad and building up on high picks. It's painful but worthwhile."

The strategies are growing in audaciousness and frequency of use. The orders from management are coming in earlier in the season, creating months of competitively compromised and often unwatchable basketball. The average margin of victory in NBA games this season is 13.1 points, the largest spread in history, and a record 89 games have been decided by 30 or more points.

All the while, the uncertainty of Antetokounmpo's future in Milwaukee lingered. The Bucks engaged in trade talks ahead of the Feb. 5 trade deadline but chose to hold on to him, even as it became increasingly clear that they didn't have much hope of even elevating into the play-in race. Milwaukee is now headed to the draft lottery for the first time since 2016, snapping a streak of nine consecutive years in the playoffs. The Bucks haven't won a postseason series since 2022. Antetokounmpo, who is under contract for one more season, has played in a career-low 36 games and privately feuded with the organization for several months, culminating in rebuking the team's requests to shut down in the final month of the season and setting up another contentious summer.

stories.headline: Summer transfer window: Grading big signings in men's soccer
stories.summary: The 2026 summer transfer window has closed. Here is how we rated the biggest deals.
stories.body:
Premier League clubs spent a record £3 billion ($4 billion) in a 2025 summer transfer window that finished with a bang thanks to Liverpool's £125 million ($169 million) signing of Newcastle United striker Alexander Isak. But with a FIFA World Cup in the middle of the window in 2026, will things stay the same?

The window opened on June 15 for the Premier League and July 1 for most of the other major European leagues.

Here are grades for all the major confirmed transfers in the men's game, with each listed by date and then by highest fee.

All fees are reported unless confirmed with an asterisk.

Sept. 1

Enzo Fernández

£125M ($169M)
Chelsea: A+

Manchester City: C

After a long summer of "will they, won't they," Man City finally stumped up an astronomical joint-British record fee to sign Fernández, reuniting him with Enzo Maresca, who managed him at Chelsea. While the Argentina international is a quality player, this is still something of an odd signing, as he thrives most as an attacking midfielder ... and City already have huge talents in Phil Foden and Rayan Cherki.

It's an incredible deal from the perspective of Chelsea perspective, who have somehow ended up with £5 million more than the asking price they set in that mid-August deadline for a player who was outwardly desperate to leave and for whom there was only one club interested.

Iliman Ndiaye

£60M ($81M)
Everton: A

Manchester City: B-

Ndiaye seemed ripe for a big Premier League move this summer; the only surprise is that it took so long for a suitor to come knocking. The 26-year-old is an electric dribbler and exciting player in the final third who is proven in England's top tier, so £60 million looks about right for this deal.

City will have felt they were light in the wing department following Sávio's departure and Jack Grealish's expected exit. Signing Ndiaye adds quality, bolsters the numbers and ensures there isn't too much pressure placed on fellow new face Allan Elias as he adapts following his move from Brazil.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo

€60M (£51M; $70M)
Lille: A

Newcastle United: B-

Fernandez-Pardo exploded onto the scene last season, scoring eight goals and registering five goals in Ligue 1 initially as a winger, then as a striker later in the campaign. He is lightning fast -- Gradient Sports clocked him at 35.51 km/h last season, making him one of the quickest players in the world -- and while there are areas of his game that need developing, he's 21, so that's to be expected.

€4M ($5M)
Borussia Monchengladbach: B

Strasbourg: B-

It is last-chance saloon for the third year running for USMNT forward Reyna, who has struggled with injury and poor form since bursting onto the scene at Borussia Dortmund in 2019. One goal and one assist in 20 games for Gladbach suggests that he didn't settle and they've done well to move him on for a fee, albeit a loss on their €7 million investment.

Seven years in the Bundesliga means Reyna was keen to experience a new style and Strasbourg will surely give him the chance to prove he can replicate his international form for a club. He shone at the 2026 World Cup and if he can repeat that, a pathway to a possible move to Strasbourg's parent-club Chelsea could be in the offing. Offering an injury-prone player a five-year contract does seem straight out of their playbook.

Aug. 3

Jordan Henderson

Free
Brentford: B

Chelsea: C+

Chelsea made it clear they wanted to sign an experienced midfielder this summer, first targeting 32-year-old Granit Xhaka at Sunderland, before successfully landing Jordan Henderson, 36, from Brentford. It's one that took the whole footballing world by surprise.

Clearly, the Blues want a few positive, experienced presences in the dressing room to counterbalance the young makeup of their squad. Henderson will certainly help maintain standards and encourage those who need it, while probably enjoying some late cameos to see out games.

Aug. 2

Randal Kolo Muani

€38M ($44M)
PSG: A

Juventus C+

Kolo Muani spent a successful six months on loan at Juventus in 2025, scoring eight goals and making a huge impact. He has much been trying to find his way back there ever since ... so, mission accomplished. He does so in what is clearly the worst form of his career, though, having scored just one league goal all of last season while on loan at Tottenham Hotspur.

Juve must be very confident they can spark him back into life, because a fee of €38 million, plus another €12 million in potential add-ons, is a lot to stake on a striker who has not played well for quite a while.

Aug. 1

Danny Welbeck

Undisclosed
Brighton & Hove Albion: C

Chelsea: A

Welbeck's move to Chelsea for a small fee is a big shock at first glance -- he's 35 years old and seemed likely to see out his Premier League career with Brighton -- but dig a little deeper and you can grasp the thinking at play here.

The Englishman remains a handy goal scorer (23 league goals in his past two seasons) and is a clever forward, capable of linking with the midfield and creating chances. He's the sort of veteran presence the Blues have been crying out for and an ideal third man in the striking corps.

July 30

Maxence Lacroix

£52M ($69M)
Crystal Palace: B

Chelsea: B

Lacroix's two seasons at Crystal Palace were incredible. He helped them to three trophies in that span -- their first silverware for decades -- and rose to the fore as a commanding voice in defense and a leader in the dressing room.

This is exactly the type of presence Chelsea -- a team with a low average age and a terrible disciplinary record -- have been crying out for. The France international has played in a back four for Wolfsburg and his country, and a back three for Palace. He'll fit whatever new Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso decides to do.

Carlos Espí

€25M ($28.8M)
Levante: B+

Real Madrid: B

Espí burst onto the LaLiga scene last season with 11 goals in just 1,340 league minutes. He is just 21, but he has a bulldozing frame and playing style that causes chaos among defenses and in the penalty box. He will replace Gonzalo García, who moved to Fulham for €40 million, as the "Joselu" option for manager José Mourinho, meaning something a bit different for late in games.

Levante will sorely miss him, naturally, as he is the perfect striker for what is likely to be another relegation scrap in 2026-27. Still, he has the second-most expensive departure in the club's history and will go a long way to servicing some hefty debts.

John Stones

Free
Manchester City: B

Inter: A

Stones' Man City exit was long in the making, so the club have had plenty of time to refresh the center back corps and prepare for his departure. Thanks to Marc Guéhi and Abdukodir Khusanov, they're very well set.

Italy -- and specifically Inter -- is a great next destination for the 32-year-old, where the league's less intense nature will be easier on his body. He should really enjoy playing as part of the Nerazzurri's back three.

July 25

Lee Kang-In

€35M ($40M)
Paris Saint-Germain: C+

Atlético Madrid: B

Lee Kang-In is a measure of how hard it is to break into PSG's first-choice XI. Despite being an excellent player, he never really got anywhere near it, often settling for the less important games on the schedule. Now he returns to LaLiga where he starred for Mallorca (2021-23).

The €35 million fee -- which could rise to €40m with bonuses -- looks on the cheap side for a player of his talent, age (25) and international marketing pull, but there is one thing holding it back from an A grade: Longtime Atlético manager Diego Simeone has a history of struggling to get the best out of playmakers like Lee, so there are no guarantees the deal will work out.

July 24

Crysencio Summerville

£55M ($73M)
West Ham United: A+

Al Hilal: B

Al Hilal have made the first big Saudi Pro League splash in the market this summer, outbidding AS Roma for Summerville in a deal that could reach £65 million if add-ons are met. Evidently, the club are keen to upgrade their forward line given Karim Benzema is 38 and Darwin Núñez's transfer hasn't worked out.

For West Ham, this is a phenomenal fee: Much more than Roma could offer, and probably more than any Premier League side would have paid. This, combined with the £85 million received for Mateus Fernandes, has not only balanced the books after relegation but also allowed them to sign star forward Jarrod Bowen to a new deal.

July 23

Elliot Anderson

£116M ($153M)
Nottingham Forest: A+

Manchester City: B-

Anderson's blockbuster move to Man City would've made him the most expensive British player of all time, if not for Chelsea's £117 million signing of Morgan Rogers on Tuesday. Nevertheless, it's a club-record signing for City.

The 23-year-old is an exceptional midfielder who can do it all: He won the most duels (297) in the league last season by a distance, yet also clocked up the most touches (3,308) and took Forest's set pieces too. He was at the heart of everything they did.

But to live up to this pricetag, he'll need to up the ante even further and sustain it for years. This kind of fee places immense pressure on a player, so there's no shortage of risk for City here.

Christos Tzolis

€40M (£35M, $45.7M)
Club Brugge: B+

Arsenal: B

Tzolis enjoyed two prolific seasons with Club Brugge in the Belgian league while holding his own in the Champions League. He is a nippy presence on the left flank and will likely assume Leandro Trossard's minutes, who moved to Bestikas for £15.3 million.

The €40 million fee is a Belgian Pro League record departure, yet it's only a modest gamble for a top Premier League club. The questions that will define if Tzolis is a success in north London are: Can his production translate to a higher level, and can he provide Mikel Arteta with the reliable tactical pliability Trossard did?

Karim Adeyemi

€22M ($25M)
Borussia Dortmund: B

Barcelona: C+

First Anthony Gordon, now Adeyemi: It's very clear that Barcelona targeted raw speed from the flanks this summer. There's no doubt the German has it, but the question is whether there's enough to his wider game to be good enough for the Catalan giants.

He's a very inconsistent performer and an unreliable presser, the latter of which feels like a big focus of manager Hansi Flick's. At least the fee -- €22 million, potentially rising to €29 million -- is modest, so Adeyemi has a chance to impress without battling too much pressure.

Alejandro Garnacho

Loan
Chelsea: B-

Aston Villa: B

Garnacho is a player Aston Villa manager Unai Emery has wanted for over a year now. The 22-year-old is the type of winger -- fast, runs in behind and keeps the touchline wide to stretch the pitch -- that Villa do not have, so his addition makes sense.

Chelsea would have much preferred this to be a permanent deal but, due to a very complex situation involving UEFA financial settlement agreements and rules on swap deals, Villa could not agree to one. This transfer could become permanent if Garnacho makes a certain number of appearances -- but as the Harvey Elliott debacle last season showed, nothing is guaranteed.

July 22

Casemiro

Free
Manchester United: B-

Inter Miami: B

Casemiro's time at Man United was a true rollercoaster. When he announced his exit in January it may have felt like a relief for the fans, but then by the end of the season, they were left wondering how they would replace the nine (!) league goals he chipped in with in 2025-26.

Now 34, he is visibly slow across the pitch and struggles to play in big spaces. Presumably that is less of an issue in MLS, which is several steps down from the Premier League, but it is something to watch with keen interest.

July 21

Morgan Rogers

£117M ($158M)
Aston Villa: A+

Chelsea: C+

Three weeks after Manchester City broke the record for a British player in Elliot Anderson, Chelsea broke it again -- by £1 million -- to sign Rogers. The 23-year-old enjoyed a brilliant season, contributing 25 goals and assists to Aston Villa's cause as they finished inside the top four and won the Europa League, and featured for England at the 2026 World Cup.

Still, this is a gargantuan move that carries immense risk, regardless of how good the player is, as far more often than not, forwards tend to fall short of the expectation this sort of fee creates.

For Villa, it's a literal jackpot. They're under pressure to generate revenue under the terms of their UEFA settlement agreement, and £117 million is an absolute game-changer. A fee of this size opens up a world of transfer possibilities for them.

July 20

João Gomes

£34M ($46M)
Wolves: C

Aston Villa: A

For roughly the same fee as Youri Tielemans left for (£35 million), Villa have signed Gomes as his replacement. The Brazil midfielder should prove a snug fit in Unai Emery's system, as he progresses the ball well and has the athleticism to track and tackle runners.

The fee, which could rise to £38 million with add-ons, looks cheap for a talented 25-year-old with 10 caps for Brazil and three seasons of Premier League football under his belt. Wolves fans are understandably unhappy with the return.

July 17

Johan Manzambi

£50M ($67M)
Freiburg: A+

Aston Villa: B+

Newcastle agreed a fee for Switzerland's World Cup star Manzambi, but Aston Villa stole in to match the terms and convince the player to join them instead. The 20-year-old had an excellent season with Freiburg -- which culminated in losing the Europa League final to Villa, coincidentally -- and looks a fine young attacking talent.

Just over £50 million is simultaneously good value for Villa, who have shopped outside the Premier League to avoid absurd markups on prices, and an amazing deal for Freiburg, who have more than doubled their record departure, which was previously €25 million for Kevin Schade.

July 16

Mason Greenwood

€39M ($45M)
Marseille: C

Fenerbahce: B

Greenwood's production at Marseille -- 37 goals and 12 assists across two Ligue 1 campaigns -- was phenomenal. For a while, he achieved star status at a club that is notoriously dysfunctional and difficult to remain consistent at.

But heavy praise turned to heavy criticism earlier this year, and for the second time in two years, he has departed a club under a cloud of off-field issues. Marseille have lost a very good striker in negative circumstances, made all the worse by the fact Manchester United took €12.5 million of the fee due to a clause in his 2024 exit from the club.

July 14

Luka Vuskovic

£46M ($61M)
Tottenham Hotspur: B

Brighton: B

Vuskovic is an extremely promising young center back, who was named Bundesliga Rookie of the Month four times last season while on loan at Hamburg, before forcing his way into Croatia's 2026 World Cup squad. He's a titan in the air and a confident ball carrier out from the back.

There is a distinct chance that Spurs have let a superb player go too soon here, and when a savvy club like Brighton want your top prospect, it's usually a signal. But they're in win-now mode and have effectively chosen to roll with experience over potential, so it's Vuskovic out and Jan Paul van Hecke in.

Youri Tielemans

£35M ($47M)
Aston Villa: C+

Manchester United: A-

After Éderson's £35 million transfer from Atalanta collapsed, United moved fast to secure Tielemans for the same fee via a release clause. For a player of this established quality and consistency it is a relative bargain -- although at 29, it's no long-term solution.

The Belgium international midfielder was generally superb for Aston Villa over his three years there and the team visibly missed him when injuries forced him to miss games. If there's a silver lining here, it's that he was reportedly a high earner and the club are under pressure to cut costs under a UEFA settlement agreement.

July 13

Andrey Santos

£48M ($64M)
Chelsea: C+

Manchester United: B+

Understandably put off by the fees paid to sign Mateus Fernandes (£85 million), Sandro Tonali (£92.5 million) and Elliot Anderson (£116 million), Man United have found a significantly cheaper way to bolster their midfield with proven Premier League quality.

Andrey Santos, 22, stepped into the Chelsea XI regularly last season and, over the course of nearly 2,500 minutes, showcased good passing and excellent tackling. He's hardly the kind of player the Blues should be looking to lose, but perhaps there's just not enough football to go around next season as the team isn't in Europe.

July 11

Morten Hjulmand

€40M ($46M)
Sporting CP: B

Atlético Madrid: A-

Long linked to Manchester United while Rúben Amorim was in charge, Hjulmand has finally made the move to one of Europe's top leagues with Atlético. Diego Simeone will love his combativeness, fire, leadership qualities and strength in the air.

A fee of €40 million, plus some modest bonuses, looks a little on the lean side as fees go for Sporting, but the reality is this was probably the maximum you'd get for the 27-year-old once interest from the big-spending Premier League clubs' dropped.

Jeremy Monga

£10M ($13M)
Leicester City: B

Manchester City: B

City outbid Arsenal to secure Monga, who has made the breakthrough to men's football incredibly early. He became the second-youngest Premier League player ever in 2025, aged 15 years and 271 days, and played just shy of 1,000 Championship minutes last season aged 16.

Anyone who makes this kind of leap is worth a look for an elite club, as they could become a homegrown superstar. Whether or not the first-team pathway ever opens up for Monga to impress at City is another question, though.

July 6

Sandro Tonali

£92.5M ($125M)
Newcastle United: A+

Tottenham Hotspur: C-

Tottenham have signed Tonali in a deal that could rise to £100 million with achievable add-ons. It's an astonishing deal and, quite frankly, an astonishing use of £100 million, making him one of the 15 most expensive footballers of all time.

Clearly, Spurs manager Roberto De Zerbi is convinced he can work miracles with his Italian compatriot, but Newcastle likely can't believe their luck. They got just one consistently strong season out of three from Tonali, before offloading him for twice what they spent to acquire him.

July 5

Denzel Dumfries

€20M ($22.8M)
Inter Milan: C

Real Madrid: A

Dumfries is one of the most prolific goalscoring defenders in world football -- although labeling him a defender may be a stretch. A direct, attacking wing back, who spends more time in the opposition box than his own, he can be a real difference-maker from the flank. Losing him for just €20 million via a release clause in his contract is tough for Inter, although the Dutchman's injury issues last season did force the Nerazzurri to learn how to cope without him.

July 3

Nathaniel Brown

€55M ($64M)
Eintracht Frankfurt: A

Bayern Munich: B

Brown's career is moving fast. He used a sensational 2025-26 season with Frankfurt to not only gatecrash Germany's 2026 World Cup squad, but oust David Raum as first-choice left back.

The 23-year-old defender is athletic, very fast, defends one-on-ones well and combines traditional overlapping runs with modern, inverted runs into the box. Born in Bavaria, his signing for Bayern is both a headline move and a homecoming.

Frankfurt won't be able to replace his quality like-for-like, but they have at least secured a fee that makes Brown one of the three most expensive left backs of all time.

July 2

Mateus Fernandes

£85M ($112M)
West Ham United: A+

Tottenham Hotspur: C+

Despite consecutive relegations from the Premier League with Southampton and then West Ham, it is clear Fernandes is an excellent player. An all-round midfielder who can pretty much do it all by the age of 21, there is no doubt Tottenham are looking in the right area here as they seek to improve their midfield.

The price, however, is eye-popping. Even Manchester United, who spent last summer shelling out roughly £65 million per attacker, had to dip out of this race for Fernandes because the quoted transfer price was so high. The Portugal midfielder will have to do incredibly well, for a long time, to prove worth this outlay.

July 1

Anthony Gordon

€70M (£60M, $80M)
Newcastle: A-

Barcelona: B

With legendary goal scorer Robert Lewandowski gone on a free transfer and Manchester United loanee Marcus Rashford far from certain to stay permanently, Barcelona needed a big addition to their forward line this summer. Gordon plays both left wing and striker, presses hard and was the fastest player in the Premier League last season, topping 36 km/h, per Gradient Sports. He's a good fit for Hansi Flick's tactical style.

This is about the right price range for any player of this established quality. Newcastle could earn an extra €10 million if add-ons are met, making this potentially even more lucrative for them.

Marco Palestra

€60M (£48M, $68M)
Atalanta: A

Chelsea: B

If Chelsea intend to play with fully fledged wing backs under new manager Xabi Alonso, signing Palestra makes a lot of sense. The 21-year-old is tall, fast and loves to knock the ball past an opponent -- but he also has neat footwork in tight spaces. The Blues are once again trusting their talent ID, staking a big transfer fee on a player with just one full season under his belt, which came on loan at Cagliari.

Naturally, Atalanta are the big winners here: They watched a player blossom out on loan, become the subject of a bidding war between Inter Milan and Chelsea, and then accepted the highest bid.

Marc Cucurella

€55M (£47M, $64M)
Chelsea: C-

Real Madrid: A-

When Chelsea's ownership group drew up their transfer strategy, this is surely not what it was supposed to look like. Cucurella is one of the few signings that has unequivocally succeeded, yet here they are losing him for a fairly modest fee, potentially rising to €60M with add-ons.

The Blues' loss is Madrid's gain: Barcelona academy graduate Cucurella returns to Spain as a fully fledged international and trophy winner, shoring up the left-back area in Madrid nicely. José Mourinho will love his blood-and-thunder style.

Ismael Saibari

€55M ($64M)
PSV Eindhoven: A

Bayern Munich: B

Saibari has blossomed over the last two years, contributing 52 goals and assists for PSV in the Champions League and Eredivisie play and securing his place as Morocco's first-choice striker. He scored at the 2026 World Cup to further enhance his reputation.

Bayern will appreciate those scoring numbers, but they will also love his ability to drop deep, receive the ball and create. It's what Harry Kane already does for them to a world class level, and now Bayern have found a very capable backup. It's a good stylistic fit for the German giants, while for PSV, it's a club record departure.

Piero Hincapié

€40M (£34.5M; $46M)
Bayer Leverkusen: C

Arsenal: A

Hincapié's loan to Arsenal has become a permanent move after certain conditions were met. He proved an excellent pickup last summer, ably sharing the left-back role with Riccardo Calafiori and covering at center back too.

Factoring in the initial loan fee of €6 million, this looks to have cost the Gunners just shy of €50 million all in. For a player of this established quality and age (24), it goes down as an absolute bargain.

Emmanuel Emegha

€25M (£22M; $29M)
Strasbourg: B

Chelsea: B

Chelsea struck a deal to sign Emegha in the summer of 2025, but opted to let him stay at sister club Strasbourg and continue developing for another year. It was a good idea, but things didn't go to plan as the Dutchman missed most of last season due to injury.

For a player who stands at 6-foot-5, he is extremely fast, with great movement, but he is unreliable in front of goal and underperformed his xG by three in 2024-25. Emegha has huge potential and is still only 23, but he probably isn't ready to start for Chelsea just yet.

Robert Lewandowski

Free transfer
Barcelona: B

Chicago Fire FC: B+

The Chicago Fire won the race to sign legendary striker Lewandowski, who may be into his late 30s but still scored 14 goals from 17 starts in LaLiga last season. He'll join MLS top scorer Hugo Cuypers (13 goals this term) in what is now a fearsome front two on paper.

It was certainly time for him to depart Barcelona, where he excelled since joining in 2022, but also accounted for a huge portion of the wage bill at a club that's been right up against it financially for some time.

Bernardo Silva

Free
Manchester City: D

Real Madrid: A

Silva, who is one of the most tactically versatile and intelligent players the sport has ever seen, was linked strongly to each of Spain's big three clubs. But Los Blancos will benefit hugely from his presence in a variety of ways.

After nine incredible years at City, there was little need for the club to recoup any sort of fee for him, but this one still really hurts. The Portugal midfielder was a crucial component of the team and the dressing room and a symbol of the Pep Guardiola era.

Ibrahima Konaté

Free
Liverpool: D

Real Madrid: B-

Konaté's athleticism is off the charts, and when he's in good form, he's close to unbeatable at the back. But inconsistency has long troubled his game, and reports in Spain suggest not only has he earned a huge signing bonus of €20 million, but he's more than tripled his weekly wage with this move.

From Madrid's perspective, this is no free transfer. But from Liverpool's perspective it is. They get absolutely nothing in return for a very good player, but have at least covered themselves for this eventuality with new €70 million arrival Jérémy Jacquet (agreed in January).

Antoine Griezmann

Free
Atletico Madrid: B

Orlando City: A

Griezmann's long farewell to Atlético was a tearjerker, and it feels right that the 35-year-old forward opted for a new challenge, on a different continent, rather than moved to another European club. He was a great servant to the club for a long time, negating the need to receive any kind of fee for him.

Orlando have had a poor campaign to date and could use all the help they can get; Griezmann's quality and personality is a great start to turning things around.

June 30

Gonçalo Ramos

€74M ($84M)
PSG: A

AC Milan: C+

First, Milan appointed former Manchester United manager Rúben Amorim as coach. Then they handed him his first new weapon: Ramos, a Champions League winner and a potent goal scorer -- albeit via a bit-part role with PSG these past three years.

This is a gargantuan outlay from the Italian giants, who have smashed their transfer record by more than €20 million for a player who has too often found himself kicking his heels for club and country of late. PSG, meanwhile, have banked €74 million, potentially rising to around €80 million, for a squad player; they'll rightly be delighted with that.

Alejandro Grimaldo

€20M ($22.7M)
Bayer Leverkusen: C

Atlético Madrid: A

Grimaldo will finally play in Spain's top tier, having left Barcelona's academy in 2016 without a first-team appearance to his name. He's blossomed abroad, at both Benfica and Bayer Leverkusen, developing into one of the best attacking fullbacks in the game. At €20 million, this is a steal for Atleti -- even if he is 30 years old.

Leverkusen don't stand a chance of replacing his quality like-for-like with a humble fee, and they've reluctantly said goodbye to one of their best players during that famous unbeaten title run in 2023-24.

June 18

Jan Paul van Hecke

£52M ($70M)
Brighton & Hove Albion: B+

Tottenham: B

Van Hecke has slowly developed into one of the Premier League's best center backs. The Netherlands international has long been one of the best passers and dribblers from the back, and now he's become a sturdier, meaner defender, too.

At 25, he's ready for the next step, and reuniting with manager Roberto De Zerbi at Tottenham feels like a brilliant match. Brighton were resigned to losing him given he had just one year left on his contract and did well to hold out for a fee above £50 million.

Víctor Muñoz

€40M (£35M; $46M)
Osasuna: B+

Liverpool: B-

Muñoz is an incredibly busy, buzzing winger who tears around the pitch, tries to beat defenders one-on-one and shoots willingly. Stylistically that makes him a good fit for Andoni Iraola, but Liverpool are gambling slightly on the 23-year-old stepping up to the elite level quickly.

For Osasuna, this is a record departure -- but not quite the huge payday it looks like. They only hold 50% of the player's rights, with Real Madrid holding the other half; that means half €40M fee will go to Los Blancos.

June 15

Marcos Senesi

Free
Bournemouth: D

Tottenham: A

Senesi was one of the outstanding center backs in the Premier League last season. A committed defender, a physical presence and a brilliant passer from the back, he stood out as one of the best free agents heading into the summer, and Spurs have won the race for his signature.

His signing does raise some questions for the club to answer. Will captain Cristian Romero be departing? Is the plan to play with two left-footers (Senesi and Micky van de Ven), or will it be a back three? Though none of that detracts from the fact this deal is a coup.

Andy Robertson

Free
Liverpool: B

Tottenham: B

Tottenham came close to signing Robertson in January and have now finally sealed the deal. The 32-year-old defender's time at Liverpool had come to a natural end as he passed his peak and Milos Kerkez replaced him in the XI.

Roberto De Zerbi will value the Scotland international's passing ability and the Spurs squad badly need his leadership qualities -- although they have reportedly paid a premium in wages for a player who won't necessarily be first choice.

June 29

Rasmus Højlund

€44M (£38M; $51M)
Manchester United: B+

Napoli: B+

Højlund's loan to Napoli was made permanent the moment the Italian giants qualified for the Champions League. The Denmark striker led the attacking line all season long, contributing 16 goals in total, and rebounded well from his disappointing spell at Man United.

It's a good deal for both clubs, as €44 million (plus a €6 million loan fee last season) for a reliable goal scorer represents strong value for Napoli, while United will be pleased to make a fair chunk of their money back on a signing that cost them an initial €75 million and simply did not work out.

stories.headline: One in three? 5%? Don't bother?! Each finalist's chance of winning the 2026 premiership
stories.summary: Play out the finals series 100 times, and how many times does each finalist win the premiership? Rohan Connolly has done the maths to determine each club's chance of winning the 2026 flag.
stories.body:
Eight teams left, eight chances to win an AFL premiership. Well, ostensibly perhaps. Like in George Orwell's "Animal Farm", we all know "some are more equal than others". And in this version, it's about both institutionalised disadvantage, and more simply, about quality.

Two teams -- Western Bulldogs and Carlton -- will have to win a historic five games to take out the flag thanks to the new Wildcard system. The top four, meanwhile, could play just three.

Perhaps too much rest could claim them, though, as has happened to a disproportionate number of qualifying final winners in preliminary finals since the introduction of the pre-finals bye in 2016.

Systems, numbers, percentages, any minuscule advantage -- they're all a massive part of finals calculations. So we thought we'd estimate your team's premiership chance expressed as a percentage. Don't like it? Don't call us. Take out your calculator and have a crack yourself.

Brisbane: 35%
There are eerie similarities between these Lions, shooting for a third flag in a row, and those of 20-plus years ago, who famously did just that, not least their capacity to peak at the perfect moment. Brisbane was 6-6 and in ninth spot after 12 games; they've since won 10 of their last 11, the last four by an average of 10 goals, and are two wins from a grand final spot. Even a qualifying final loss on the SCG to the Swans wouldn't faze them unduly, both their flags have been won playing every week of September. Brisbane has the most talented list, no injury concerns, knows exactly what needs to be done, and has done it, with plenty to spare twice already. The Lions have to be seen as the best premiership chance right now.

Fremantle: 32%
It's been some sort of season for the Dockers, who've only dropped four games, and two of those relatively meaningless after having sewn up top spot. They now have the perfect pathway for a Perth team - two Optus Stadium finals (where they've won all 12 games this year) en route to grand final day. Never underestimate, though, the challenges for WA teams in winning big games at the still relatively unfamiliar surrounds of the MCG, a venue at which Freo plays on average just two games a season, and at which their recent record is 2-3. They're good enough, of course, they've proved that. But against more seasoned finals campaigners, they're going to need to be.

Hawthorn: 10%
A big premiership probability drop to the next most likely chance. Why? Well, winning a final in Perth is tough, the Hawks' recent form has been less than stellar, and indeed Carlton is the only decent side they've beaten in the second half of the season. That said, another against-the-odds Perth final win (they've done it twice before and demolished West Coast there last start) would land them in an MCG preliminary final. They're also in great shape on the availability front, Conor Nash the only first-choice player unavailable, and Will Day finally ready to take part in a big finals campaign. Will take some doing, but you wouldn't say they couldn't.

Geelong: 8%
The Cats were in strife three-quarters of the way through the season after five losses in six games. Of course, as they have so often, they found a way through, winning their last six. They're solid everywhere, too, ranked No.1 for defence, third for attack, and are the undisputed best territory team in the competition. The experience factor goes without saying, this being Geelong's 14th finals campaign in 16 years under Chris Scott. Even injuries might be coming into line, star midfielder Max Holmes an outside chance to play against the Blues this week. One concern, perhaps, is their early finals draw, the Cats having lost three of their last four against Carlton, and to both Fremantle and Hawthorn, their potential semifinal opponents.

Sydney: 6%
Obviously, this rating would have been considerably higher had it not been for the events at the Pullman Hotel, and the suspensions of five players, including three of the Swans' best half-dozen in Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey. The disgrace has cost Sydney class in all parts of the ground, possession power and scoring potency, Heeney and Warner having contributed more than 60 goals between them this season. The AFL's highest-scoring team does still have Coleman medallist Charlie Curnow and Logan McDonald, though, who have booted more than 100. The form of Errol Gulden and potential return of midfielder Justin McInerney will be critical. Two home finals, where the Swans have won 10 of their last 11 and beat Brisbane early this season, doesn't hurt, either.

Adelaide: 4%
There's plenty of heat on the Crows and coach Matthew Nicks already after last year's disastrous straight sets exit at home after having finished on top of the ladder. A 15-8 record this season isn't shabby, of course, and Adelaide is strong defensively and in contested ball, two finals staples. But the home finals advantage doesn't weigh as heavily, given last September and the fact four of the Crows' eight losses this year have come at home. One big plus will be the very in-form Izak Rankine, suspended last year, skipper Jordan Dawson has been superb all season, and Taylor Walker's impending retirement might provide an emotional boost, too, but a flag won with the last three legs won on the road would be a huge effort.

Carlton: 3%
I know, I know, given that the Blues have won 12-and-a-half of their last 15 games, the best form line in the competition, three per cent seems harsh indeed. But there's several things to take into consideration. Pathway is perhaps the most important. We're talking about history, here. No side previously has won five white-hot finals to land a premiership. Indeed, only North Melbourne (in 1977) has played five to do it, and that included a loss and a draw. And yes, the Blues have a good record against Geelong, but win this week and it's either a trip to Perth to play the Dockers or an MCG clash with Hawthorn, who've beaten them -- comfortably -- on the past four occasions. Win that, and it's a preliminary final in either Brisbane or Sydney. To say that's a big ask is an understatement.

Western Bulldogs: 2%
Sneaking into eighth spot then surviving a post-siren kick against the ninth-placed team isn't a great CV when you're chasing a premiership. Nor is a record of 3-8 and a draw against your final eight opponents. Nor a dismal ranking of 14th offensively and a mediocre ninth defensively. Nor the likely absence this week of key midfielder Tom Liberatore and confirmed absence of another in Matt Kennedy. Then having to win in Adelaide followed by either Sydney or Brisbane just to get to a preliminary final. Needless to say the Dogs will need their biggest guns, namely Marcus Bontempelli, Ed Richards, Aaron Naughton, Tim English and Bailey Dale, to produce their absolute best and then some if the Dogs are to pull out a premiership miracle.

You can read more of Rohan Connolly's work at FOOTYOLOGY.

stories.headline: Ferrari to run Michael Schumacher tribute livery at Italian Grand Prix
stories.summary: Ferrari will mark the 30-year anniversary of Michael Schumacher's arrival at Maranello by running a special livery at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.
stories.body:
Ferrari will mark the 30-year anniversary of Michael Schumacher's arrival at Maranello by running a special livery at this weekend's Italian Grand Prix.

The cars will feature a livery that is inspired by the 1996 Ferrari F310 that Schumacher drove in his debut season with the Italian team.

Schumacher won five of his seven titles with Ferrari as well as taking 72 race victories -- more than any other driver with the team.

He joined Ferrari from Benneton in 1996 as a two-time world champion and announced his first retirement from F1 following his penultimate victory for Ferrari at the 2006 Italian Grand Prix.

The cars of Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc in Monza will be predominantly red, with hints of gold on the wheels that pay homage to the all-gold wheels of the 1996 car.

Schumacher's logo will feature on the car as well as seven stars on the nose that echo the design the seven-time champion wore on the top of his helmet while racing at Ferrari following his final title in 2004.

- Lewis Hamilton takes ownership of iconic Ferrari F40 road car

- Italian Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions

Hamilton and Leclerc will also wear racesuits designed to tie in with the look of the special livery as well as their own helmet designs.

Three of Schumacher's former Ferrari cars -- the F310 (1996), F2002 (2002) and 248 F1 (2006) -- will be present at Monza to complete demonstration laps of the circuit over the weekend.

stories.headline: Which fantasy hockey league is right for you?
stories.summary: Roto vs H2H points? Dynasty vs redraft? With all the scoring settings, roster setup and more, here's your first stop when signing up for an ESPN Fantasy Hockey league.
stories.body:
So you've decided to take the fantasy hockey plunge, joining millions of others in enjoying one of the sporting world's best game within a game. Welcome. Or perhaps you've already waded through these puck-friendly fantasy waters and feel inspired to dive into a different type of pool. Preseason greetings to you too. Either way, leaving other customizable options (roster size, lineup rules, bench flexibility, IR spots etc.) alone for now, here's a rundown of ESPN Fantasy's variety of fantasy hockey leagues, available to suit any taste.

H2H Points

The most popular game in ESPN's fantasy hockey universe pits individual managers against others in weekly head-to-head fisticuffs with a slew of weighted points at stake. Most total points wins the week 1-0 - no fuss, no muss. While always customizable to your own statistical taste, our default 12-category game presents as follows:

Goals (G) 2
Assists (A) 1
Power Play Points (PPP) .5
Short Handed Points (SHP) .5
Shots on Goal ( SOG) .1
Hits (HIT) .1
Blocked Shots (BLK) .5
Goaltender Wins (W) 4
Goals Against (GA) -2
Saves (SV) .2
Shutouts (SO) 3
Overtime Losses (OTL) 1

In stride with this formula, skaters who shoot regularly, score plentifully, and contribute often on the power play, qualify as fantasy royalty. But those characters are limited in number. Once the elite are spoken for, especially on larger fantasy rosters, there's much to appreciate about prolific shot-blockers who also chip in on offense on occasion. Think defenseman Jacob Trouba. An evening's haul including an assist, three hits, four shots, and three blocked, and -- without much obvious fantasy fanfare -- he's racked up 3.1 fantasy points. An above-average haul by any fantasy measure.

Furthermore, not unlike in the living, breathing game itself, goaltending matters. There are too many fantasy points at stake to pooh-pooh the position. While having good goaltending won't ensure a triumphant turn by April, rolling out sub-mediocre players on weak teams most certainly guarantees the opposite. Doesn't matter who you have up front. Pay the role proper mind, or pay a sad fantasy price.

In considering any player, spending a few moments in assessing the individual, by doing a little bit of simple arithmetic -- what is their potential fantasy sum? -- is the most sure-fire way to earn rich fantasy dividends in H2H points leagues. Whether it's during the draft or in evaluating free agent/trade commodities through the season.

H2H Categories

Varying from the H2H points formula, so-called "each" category leagues also maintain a committed, loyal following. Managers engaged in this style of contest, where stat egalitarianism reigns, are best served by striving for competitive balance. Each category, in direct head-to-head competition, is equal to each other in that goals, hits, blocked shots, whatever-your-fantasy-fancy etc. counts towards the week's final score, accruing over the course of the season. You've earned 31 shots on goal and your opponent has 30? You win that category, full stop.

Again, margin of victory in individual categories, large or small, matters not. Beating your competitor in hits by a singular check carries equal weight to obliterating them in goals. Since defeating your direct rival 10-2 in a 12 category format is a significantly bigger victory than edging them 6-5-1, you want to give yourself a competitive chance in all/most aspects of the fantasy game. Top-tier, well-rounded players are extra valuable in battling for a favorable blowout, especially on small rosters. For example, Florida's Brady Tkachuk checks a bunch of valuable boxes, night in and night out, in fantasy leagues that reward both scoring and physical play. Loading up on specialists in one category is much less useful than in other forms of H2H play. A balanced smorgasbord of skilled contributors in all aspects of the game will provide you with the greatest chance of campaign-long success.

H2H Most Categories

This type of league operates in similar fashion to "each" category competition except whichever manager emerges with the weekly victory wins 1-0. You win the week or you lose it, regardless of final tally. A 6-5-1 win is just as good as 12-0. In this case, the strategy of loading up on players who satisfy most stats, as opposed to striving for balance across the fantasy board, has merit. If you're rocking out in eight or nine of 12 categories, maybe don't sweat penalty minutes, or time-on-ice or the like too much. Securing a few "slam-dunk" categories at the expense of one or two others makes greater sense in this particular brand of fantasy play. Please don't draft a singular skater with an impressive plus/minus at the expense of nailing down shots on net. You're only increasing your odds of losing both categories.

It also bears repeating: Goaltenders cannot be shrugged off in any brand of H2H league, including this type, when more than two categories are devoted to the position. Please don't try to convince yourself otherwise.

Rotisserie (Roto)

Interested in a slow-burn, largely unforgiving league that can't be won in the first few months of the season but certainly can be lost? Willing to accept the challenge of assembling a roster with little margin for weakness, similar to how it's done IRL? Then this brand of fantasy play might be for you. As with H2H Categories competition, constructing and maintaining a balanced fantasy squad is vital in Roto leagues. Only more so. In direct competition with every other manager at all times, striving for a share of points available based on standings in individual categories, squandering one or two can prove catastrophically costly.

Sitting top spot in goals or ATOI or hits etc. in a 12-team/10-category league translates into 12 of a possible 12 points. Sitting dead last converts into a single point. That's a massive gap. Which is why ranking worst or near-bottom in a couple of stats, and subsequently earning only a point or two of a maximum of 12, is difficult to overcome, regardless of how well you're faring otherwise. By no means a gateway league, Roto competition best suits managers with strong fantasy stomachs. But that also means victory, when achieved, tastes all the sweeter after such a season-long grind.

Season Points

The ESPN Fantasy version that most closely resembles the lesser-nuanced game of your elders, where everyone gathered at the pub for an evening, armed with a pen, paper, and magazine, and selected their players for the year. Teams accrued points based on scoring and goaltending, and whichever side finished with the highest total, won.

Of course, there are many ways to cyber-customize your points league with other categories, trades, free-agent acquisitions, roster limits, and varying lineup adjustment windows. Daily or weekly, it's up to you. But the founding philosophy remains the same: the best overall team by season's end sports the crown. While this style of league lacks the charm of despising another individual manager over seven exclusive days in head-to-head combat, it -- unlike classic roto leagues -- serves as an excellent introduction for newbie managers to get their feet wet. Especially those who don't want to devote as much time, at least to start.

Dynasty/Keeper vs. Single Season

There are advantages to both. While dynasty/keeper competition is more kindred to how real teams are run -- management doesn't get to start from scratch every year in the NHL -- with redraft leagues, there's the benefit of enjoying a clean slate the following season, no matter how badly a current campaign is unfolding. But there's inarguably a greater sense of satisfaction with enjoying fantasy success on the blades of a roster built over time, from rebuild to peak performance. In stricter dynasty leagues, where few bodies move in or out, it's often nifty to maintain relationships with players from their rookie debuts, well into the veteran years. For many then, keeper competition -- middle ground between an all-in dynasty and turn-the-page redraft play -- will suit you best. Selecting six to eight keepers every campaign is a common tact, still allowing for improvement from outside help at season's onset. No one's going to relinquish Connor McDavid as a keeper, but some very good players will inevitably re-enter the draft in these modified leagues.

Again, there's no right or wrong way to play ESPN Fantasy Hockey. Depending on how much time and energy you want to invest - from the bare minimum to managing your squad as a quasi part-time job - it's all about customizing whichever league feels most up your own fantasy alley. And enjoying this great game through a fun bonus lens from late summer until it all wraps up in the spring.

Ready to play? Sign up for free today!

stories.headline: EFL criticises UEFA after rescheduling three domestic fixtures
stories.summary: The English Football League has accused UEFA of an "unwillingness to cooperate" after it says the European governing body's stance forced them to rearrange three domestic fixtures.
stories.body:
The English Football League has accused UEFA of an "unwillingness to cooperate" after it says the European governing body's stance forced them to rearrange three domestic fixtures.

Everton and Wolves were scheduled to play their Carabao Cup third-round tie on Sept. 9 before Liverpool and Atlético Madrid's Champions League clash was, on Saturday, announced for the same day.

As a result, that contest and two others -- Liverpool and Tottenham in the League Cup and Wolves vs. Portsmouth in the Championship -- have been rescheduled.

An EFL statement read: "On Saturday, UEFA announced that it had scheduled Liverpool v Atlético Madrid for the same date, despite it being clear that Everton and Liverpool cannot play home fixtures on the same evening.

"The EFL met with UEFA officials on Monday morning to explore available options, however in those discussions it was made clear that they were unwilling to consider rescheduling the Liverpool v Atlético Madrid fixture due to the impact on supporters travelling from overseas.

"Disappointingly, the League has therefore been forced to make changes.

"Over recent seasons the League has made a number of changes to accommodate the expansion of UEFA Club competitions -- a decision which was made without adequate consultation with domestic leagues.

"These changes have included splitting Carabao Cup round three ties across two weeks, and implementing draw conditions for round three which prevent scheduling conflicts for clubs playing in the UEFA Champions League and UEFA Europa League.

- Champions League draw becomes UEFA's latest stand against FIFA president Infantino

- Champions League draw: Good games for Liverpool, bad for Barcelona

"This makes UEFA's unwillingness to cooperate all the more frustrating, not least for the supporters of the five impacted clubs, and we sincerely apologise for the inconvenience caused."

UEFA, in response, insisted it "always does its best to accommodate reasonable requests", but said the "potential conflict" only emerged after fixtures were published, when changes were no longer possible.

The European governing body said in a statement: "UEFA regularly receives scheduling requests from associations, leagues and clubs and always does its best to accommodate reasonable requests wherever possible.

"In this case, no issue had been raised with UEFA during the scheduling process, and the potential conflict only became apparent after the publication of the fixture lists.

"At that stage, it was not possible to make changes, particularly given the significant number of supporters who may already have arranged international travel and accommodation. We believe that these commitments deserve to be respected.

"UEFA remains in contact with the relevant stakeholders, and we appreciate all efforts to minimise any local operational challenges."

Everton vs. Wolves is now set for Wednesday, Sept. 16; Liverpool vs. Tottenham, originally slated for Sept. 16, is now a day earlier and Wolves vs. Portsmouth, also initially due to be played on Sept. 16, will take place on Oct. 20.

stories.headline: Yeo reveals World Cup stance, contract timeline
stories.summary: Isaah Yeo is refusing to close the door on captaining Australia at the Rugby League World Cup as the Penrith lock looks to wrap up a NRL contract extension and make his comeback for the Panthers.
stories.body:
Isaah Yeo is refusing to close the door on captaining Australia at the Rugby League World Cup as the Penrith lock looks to wrap up a NRL contract extension and make his comeback for the Panthers.

Yeo has been named on an extended bench for Sunday's final regular-season game against Wests Tigers, as he aims to return from a pectoral issue that has seen him miss the last three weeks of NRL action.

The most likely scenario for Yeo is the Panthers keep him on ice until the a sudden-death final, much like Penrith did in 2023 with Jarome Luai's shoulder injury.

Yeo avoided surgery, with Penrith hoping to nurse the 31-year-old through the finals series, before deciding if and when he would go under the knife.

The World Cup, which kicks off when the Kangaroos face New Zealand on October 15, could play a factor with Yeo hopeful of featuring if he can get through Penrith's finals campaign without further aggravating his injury.

"If I get back out on the field and I can perform, then obviously I would still put my hand up for the World Cup and go from there," Yeo said.

"Obviously that's a conversation for down the track. I'm just trying to get back for Penrith at the moment and see how we go from there.

"I have never done anything like that before, so it's a little bit of the unknown. But it's travelling well. I'd like to think that bodes well, but we'll just wait and see."

Yeo's month-long absence has given the lock a chance to sit down with club powerbrokers and discuss his future.

The Panthers co-captain is a free agent on November 1, but appears set on staying put rather than testing his value on the open market.

Yeo turns 32 later this year, meaning his next deal is probably going to be his last as one of the club's top earners.

His decision to remain loyal will likely have a flow-on effect at Penrith in their quest to retain a who's who of off contract stars headlined by Nathan Cleary, Moses Leota and Liam Martin.

"There have certainly been talks and they've all been really positive. So that would be nice to get that and get back playing as well," Yeo said.

"This has obviously given me a bit of time to get that all nutted out.

"It's obviously been beneficial that I haven't been playing and I have been able to have talks like that.

"It would be nice to get back to playing and have that all sorted as well."

stories.headline: Trevino singles in go-ahead run in 8th as Reds beat wild-card chasing Padres 4-3
stories.summary: — Jose Trevino drove in the go-ahead run with a bases-loaded single in the eighth inning, lifting the Cincinnati Reds to a 4-3 victory over the San Diego Padres on Tuesday night.
stories.body:
CINCINNATI -- — Jose Trevino drove in the go-ahead run with a bases-loaded single in the eighth inning, lifting the Cincinnati Reds to a 4-3 victory over the San Diego Padres on Tuesday night.


San Diego (73-66) began the day with a half-game lead on Arizona for the third and final NL wild-card spot. The Diamondbacks hosted the Phillies later Tuesday night.


With the score tied at 2 in the eighth, the Reds loaded the bases with one out against Adrian Morejon (9-3). Trevino lined a sharp single to center, scoring Elly De La Cruz with the go-ahead run.


Juan Brito followed with a sacrifice fly to give the Reds a two-run cushion.


Emilio Pagán allowed a solo homer to Fernando Tatis, his second of the night, in the ninth but secured his 20th save.


Brock Burke (6-5) got the win for Cincinnati.


Samad Taylor tripled for the second time this season and scored on Manny Machado's sacrifice fly to put the Padres ahead 1-0 in the first.


The Reds tied it in the bottom half when Hector Rodriguez doubled and later scored on JJ Bleday's single.


Tatis put the Padres ahead 2-1 in the fifth with his 18th home run.


Reds left-hander Nick Lodolo allowed two earned runs and five hits with two walks and five strikeouts while tying a season high with 100 pitches.


Edwin Arroyo doubled in the fifth and scored on Rodriguez's single to tie it at 2.


Padres starter Randy Vazquez allowed two earned runs and five hits in 4 2/3 innings with a walk and three strikeouts.


San Diego missed a couple scoring chances late in Tuesday's game.


They had runners on first and second with no outs in the seventh, but Reds right-hander Luis Mey worked out of the jam. In the eighth, Jackson Merrill doubled with two outs, but Brock Burke struck out Luis Campusano to end the inning.


Up next
Padres RHP Casey Mize (5-8, 3.45) will face Reds LHP Brandon Williamson (2-3, 6.11) in the series finale on Wednesday.


—

stories.headline: 76ers sign 7-foot-6 center Tacko Fall, others to camp deal
stories.summary: The Philadelphia 76ers have signed Tacko Fall, Jameer Nelson Jr. and Saint Thomas to Exhibit 10 contracts.
stories.body:
The Philadelphia 76ers have signed Tacko Fall, Jameer Nelson Jr. and Saint Thomas, the team announced Tuesday. All three players are on Exhibit 10 contracts, a source familiar with their deals told ESPN, and will be a part of Sixers training camp in Camden, New Jersey, later this month.

The 7-foot-6 Fall last played in the NBA during the 2021-22 season for the Cleveland Cavaliers. Before that he was teammates with new Sixers star Jaylen Brown on the Boston Celtics from 2019 to 2021.

Fall most recently played for the Ningbo Rockets of the Chinese Basketball Association.

Nelson averaged 18.9 points on 47.5% shooting with 3.4 assists and 1.2 steals in 25 games for the G League's Stockton Kings last season. His father, Jameer Nelson Sr., is the executive vice president of basketball operations for the Sixers.

Thomas was a member of the Sixers' G League affiliate, the Delaware Blue Coats, last season. He averaged 12.5 points on 46.6% shooting with 5.0 rebounds and 3.7 assists.

stories.headline: Transfer deadline day recap: Everton hopeful on Balogun deal, Enzo signs for Man City
stories.summary: We recap the latest news, rumors, done deals and reaction throughout Europe's transfer deadline day, up to the Premier League window closing at 6 p.m. ET.
stories.body:
Quite why Premier League clubs choose to leave any transfer business until deadline day -- never mind the final hours of deadline day -- remains somewhat of a mystery, but you cannot deny that it adds intrigue and excitement for fans everywhere.

This year was no different, with Enzo Fernández's record-equaling move to Manchester City from Chelsea going to the wire and beyond as contingent moves elsewhere fell away.

Chelsea could have pulled the plug on the £125m deal but didn't - and have they left themselves light in midfield as a result?

Elsewhere, Everton seemingly failed to sign more players than they actually did land, while Tottenham Hotspur made a couple of intriguing moves, none more so than the forgotten man Mykhailo Mudryk.

It will be intriguing to see how he, and any of the other new faces, fare in the Premier League. For the accountants, lawyers and agents it's now time for a rest.

Enjoy all that happened as we brought you the latest news, rumors, done deals and reaction throughout the day.
